K-289.h1: Trace Your First Words: Three Short Fruit Names
K-289.title: First Word Tracing for Kindergarten - Fruits | Free Printable PDF
K-289.metaDescription: First word tracing worksheet: three short fruit words - pear, fig, apple - each with a solid model, a dashed copy to trace and an empty line. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-289.p1: Three fruits run down the left edge of this Kindergarten word tracing page - a pear, a fig, an apple - and no word on it is longer than five letters. Beside each picture sits a block of handwriting lines: the name printed once in solid teal on the top line, the same word repeated in dashed letters underneath, and a third line left completely empty. The child says the fruit aloud, traces the dashed copy, then writes the word alone on the blank line.
K-289.p2: Short words are the whole point of this version. Pear, fig and apple are three, three and five letters, few enough that a child who has been forming single letters can hold the entire word in mind from the first stroke to the last. Because the solid model sits directly above the dashed copy, the eye has something correct to check against at every moment, and the empty line arrives while that model is still in view rather than pages later.
K-289.p3: Print the PDF free and hand out a sharpened pencil rather than a marker, so the dashed guides stay visible under the strokes. This is the gentlest of the tracing pages: the vehicles version asks for two independent writes after a single trace, and the toys version moves up to words of eight and nine letters. When these three fruit words are steady, the singular and plural page adds an ending to words the child can already write.

K-290.h1: Trace Once, Write It Twice: Vehicle Words on Handwriting Lines
K-290.title: Trace Once Write Twice for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-290.metaDescription: Word tracing worksheet: trace each vehicle word once, then write it twice on two empty lines with only the card label left as a model. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-290.p1: The model word on this Kindergarten page has moved. Four vehicles sit in cream cards down the left - an airplane, an excavator, a tractor, a canoe - and each word is printed in solid teal under its own picture, not on the writing lines. To the right, the top line carries the word in dashed letters for one trace, and below it wait two empty lines. Trace once, then write the word twice with no letters underneath to follow.
K-290.p2: Removing the model from the line block is a small change that asks for a lot. The first write still has the traced word directly above it; the second has only the child's own attempt and a label a card-width away. That is where a teacher finds out whether the shape of the word has been learned or merely copied. Compare the two writes on each row: the same letter heights and the same spacing twice over means the word has been remembered.
K-290.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child finish one whole row before moving down, so the memory of the trace is fresh at both writes. Four rows is a longer stint than the three-row fruit version, and the words here run from five letters to nine. If two independent writes are too much, the first words page keeps a solid model on the line above every blank; if the child is ready for more, the write the word page removes the tracing altogether.

K-291.h1: Trace the Longer Words: Skateboard, Airplane, Dinosaur
K-291.title: Long Word Tracing for Kindergarten - Toys | Free Printable PDF
K-291.metaDescription: Long word tracing worksheet: three toy words of eight to ten letters, each traced once in dashed letters and then written out on two empty lines. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-291.p1: Skateboard, airplane, dinosaur. Three toys, three long words, and every one of them at least eight letters. This Kindergarten tracing page keeps the layout the shorter versions use - a picture card on the left with the word printed under it, a dashed copy to trace on the first line and empty lines beneath - but the words themselves now run most of the way across the page, so the child has to keep going long after the easy part is over.
K-291.p2: Long words are where letter formation meets stamina. A child can produce a neat three-letter word and still let a ten-letter one drift uphill, shrink at the end, or lose a letter in the middle, and this page makes all three of those visible in a single row. Size is the thing to watch: because the word must fit the line, the letters have to stay the same height from the first to the last rather than growing as the hand tires.
K-291.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child rest the pencil between words if the row was hard work; three long words done well is worth more than a page rushed. Only three rows appear here for that reason. The fruit version uses words of three to five letters if these are still too much, and the vehicles version sits between the two at four rows. After this, the write the word page asks for long words from the picture alone.

K-294.h1: Dot to Dot 1 to 10: Join Ten Dots to Finish the Picture
K-294.title: Dot to Dot 1-10 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-294.metaDescription: Dot to dot 1-10 worksheet: ten numbered dots with part of the outline already printed, so a short count still finishes a whole picture. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-294.p1: Half of the picture on this Kindergarten dot to dot is already there. A grey outline is printed across the cream panel, and only ten dots are left for the child to join: dot 1, ringed in orange, then 2, then on to 10, closing the shape at the last dot. A counting strip along the bottom shows 1 to 10 in small circles, so a child who loses the place can touch the numbers in turn and find where to go next.
K-294.p2: Ten is a short count, and pre-printing part of the outline is what makes it enough. A child who can only count reliably to ten still gets a complete picture rather than a half-finished one, which matters more at this age than the number of dots earned. The order is still the whole task: find 4 among nine other dots, draw a straight line to it, look for 5. A number skipped bends the line across the shape and shows itself immediately.
K-294.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child color the finished picture afterward. Keep a finger on the counting strip for the first two or three dots and then let go. This is the shortest of the dot to dot pages: the teen version runs from 11 to 20, and the count on version stretches to 30 with no printed outline at all. When ten dots are joined without a pause, the number line page asks for the same counting without a picture at the end.

K-295.h1: Dot to Dot 11 to 20: A Teen Number Count
K-295.title: Dot to Dot 11-20 Teen Numbers for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-295.metaDescription: Teen number dot to dot: the count starts at 11 and runs to 20, with part of the outline printed and a counting strip from 11 to 20 below. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-295.p1: The count on this Kindergarten dot to dot begins at eleven. Dot 11 carries the orange ring, and the nine dots after it climb down the panel to 20, with part of the figure already drawn in grey so the child's lines complete a shape rather than build one from nothing. The strip under the panel runs 11 to 20 instead of the usual 1 to 20, which is the clue to what this page is really practising.
K-295.p2: Teen numbers are the stretch of the count where most children slow down, and they slow down for a reason: the names stop matching the digits. Fourteen sounds like four and looks like 14, seventeen sounds like seven and looks like 17, and a child reciting from one often sails past them without ever reading them. Starting at 11 removes the run-up, so the only numbers on the page are the ones that need the work, ten of them, one after another.
K-295.p3: Print the PDF free and ask the child to read each number out loud before drawing to it, since the naming is the difficult part rather than the drawing. If the teens are new, the 1 to 10 page builds the habit on easier ground first. The count on version keeps the same start at 11 but runs all the way to 30 and prints no outline. The number of the day page then takes a single teen number apart eight different ways.

K-296.h1: Dot to Dot: Count On from 11 to 30 with No Outline
K-296.title: Count On Dot to Dot 11-30 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-296.metaDescription: Dot to dot count on worksheet: twenty dots numbered 11 to 30 and no printed outline, so every line of the picture comes from the child. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-296.p1: Nothing is printed inside the panel of this Kindergarten dot to dot except the dots themselves. Twenty of them, numbered 11 to 30, are scattered across the cream square with 11 ringed in orange, and every line of the finished picture has to come from the child's pencil. The counting strip below runs the full 11 to 30 so the sequence is available to check against, but the shape gives away nothing at all until it is drawn.
K-296.p2: Counting on from a number other than one is a different skill from reciting the count, and this page makes the difference plain: there is no 1 to fall back on and no outline to hint at where the next dot should be. Twenty steps also carry the child across the twenties, where the pattern of the number names finally becomes regular after the teens. A dot missed here leaves an obvious slash across the middle of the drawing, so the page corrects itself.
K-296.p3: Print the PDF free and leave the counting strip uncovered; reading 23 and then hunting for it is the work, not remembering it. This is the longest of the dot to dot pages. If twenty dots is too far, the teen version stops at 20, and the 1 to 10 version prints most of the outline in advance. Once the child counts on confidently to 30, the number line page asks for the same numbers to be found on a line instead of in a scatter.

K-298.h1: Copy the Grid Picture: First Steps on a 6x6 Grid
K-298.title: Copy the Grid Picture 6x6 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-298.metaDescription: Grid copying worksheet for beginners: two 6x6 pixel pictures with no letters or numbers, each beside an empty grid to copy square by square. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-298.p1: Two pictures, two empty grids, and not a letter or a number anywhere on the page. This Kindergarten grid copy worksheet gives each card a six-by-six grid with some squares filled solid teal so a simple shape appears, and an identical blank grid beside it. The child looks at the filled grid, counts across and down to find the same square on the empty one, and colors it, working through the picture square by square until the copy matches.
K-298.p2: Six by six is thirty-six squares, small enough that a child can see the whole picture at once and still find a single square in it. Leaving the edges unlabelled is deliberate at this stage: the only way to place a square is to count from the corner in both directions, which is exactly the row-and-column habit the labelled versions later put names to. A copy that bends or slides one square sideways shows where the counting stopped.
K-298.p3: Print the PDF free and offer one colored pencil rather than a set, so attention stays on position instead of on decorating. Work the top picture together and leave the second one to the child. When counting from the corner is reliable, the letters and numbers version puts A to F along the top and 1 to 6 down the side so squares can be named aloud, and the 8x8 version enlarges the grid. The grid coordinates page turns those names into the instruction.

K-299.h1: Copy the Picture Using Letters and Numbers: A to F, 1 to 6
K-299.title: Grid Copy with Letters and Numbers for Kindergarten | Free PDF
K-299.metaDescription: Labelled grid copying worksheet: A to F across the top and 1 to 6 down the side of both grids, so every square can be named before it is colored. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-299.p1: Letters run along the top of every grid on this Kindergarten page and numbers run down the side. Two cards each hold a six-by-six pixel picture on the left and an empty six-by-six grid on the right, and both grids carry the same labels: A to F across, 1 to 6 down. The child finds a filled square, reads off its letter and its number, then colors the square with that same address on the blank grid.
K-299.p2: Naming a square is what turns counting into reading a coordinate. Instead of tracking two counts in the head, the child can say C4 out loud, hold two symbols instead of two distances, and check the copy against the model without recounting from the corner every time. It is also the point at which a mistake becomes explainable: not the picture looks wrong, but I colored B3 when it should have been B4. Saying each address aloud before coloring is what makes that possible.
K-299.p3: Print the PDF free and insist on the naming for the first few squares even when the child can see where to go. Two pictures per page is enough for a first sitting. The unlabelled 6x6 version is the place to start if counting from the corner is still uncertain, and the 8x8 version keeps the labels while widening the grid to A to H and 1 to 8. From here the grid coordinates page gives the addresses and asks for the picture.

K-300.h1: Copy the Picture on an 8x8 Grid: A to H, 1 to 8
K-300.title: Copy the Grid Picture 8x8 for Kindergarten | Free Printable PDF
K-300.metaDescription: 8x8 grid copying worksheet: sixty-four squares per grid, labelled A to H and 1 to 8, with two pixel pictures to copy square by square. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-300.p1: Eight columns and eight rows make sixty-four squares, and this Kindergarten grid copy page asks the child to work through two of them. Each card shows a filled pixel picture on the left and an empty grid on the right, both labelled A to H along the top and 1 to 8 down the side. The pictures use more squares than the smaller grids do, so the copy takes longer and the child has to keep track of where the work stopped.
K-300.p2: A bigger grid changes the task in a way that is easy to underestimate. On six by six a child can hold the whole picture in view; on eight by eight the eye has to travel, and with it comes the real skill of working row by row rather than jumping to whichever filled square is noticed next. The labels make that method possible - finish row 3 across, then start row 4 - and a child who works this way finishes with a clean copy and no gaps.
K-300.p3: Print the PDF free and suggest the child crosses off each row of the model with a finger as it is finished. Expect this page to take twice as long as the six-by-six versions; it is not a warm-up. If the copy drifts, go back to the labelled 6x6 page, or to the unlabelled first steps page if the child is still counting from the corner. The grid coordinates page uses the same lettered grid but supplies codes to color instead of a picture.

K-302.h1: One and Many: First Words with Bat, Fox and Koala
K-302.title: Singular and Plural First Words - Animals | Free Printable PDF
K-302.metaDescription: Singular and plural worksheet for beginners: three animal rows, one on the left and two on the right, with the plural in dashed letters to trace. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-302.p1: Bat, fox, koala. Three rows, three animals, and one idea repeated three times on this Kindergarten singular and plural page. The left half of each row shows a single animal with a green badge reading 1 and its name printed in solid teal beneath. The right half shows the same animal twice with a badge reading 2, the plural word in dashed letters below, and an empty line under that. Two pills at the top hold the rule: 1 for one, 2 or 3 for many.
K-302.p2: Three rows is a short page on purpose. A child meeting plurals for the first time needs to see the same thing happen more than once before it becomes a rule, and three is enough for that without the writing becoming the obstacle. Two of the words simply take an s - bats, koalas - and the third, fox, takes es, which is the first hint that the ending is not always the same letter. The pictures multiply while only the end of the word changes.
K-302.p3: Print the PDF free and say each pair aloud before the pencil moves: one bat, two bats. If the child writes the plural on the empty line without glancing back at the dashed model, the ending has moved from tracing into use. The longer words version keeps the same layout but uses four rows of longer vehicle names and groups of three. The trace and write words page is the warm-up if writing a whole word is still hard work.

K-303.h1: One and Many: Longer Words with Rocket, Helicopter and Excavator
K-303.title: Singular and Plural Longer Words - Vehicles | Free Printable PDF
K-303.metaDescription: Singular and plural worksheet with longer words: four vehicle rows, one vehicle against three, and the plural traced first and then written. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-303.p1: The words on this Kindergarten singular and plural page are the long ones. Rocket, helicopter, excavator, motorcycle - four vehicles, four rows, and every plural at least seven letters by the time the s is added. One vehicle with a badge reading 1 sits on the left of each row under its printed name; three of the same vehicle sit on the right under a badge reading 3, with the plural in dashed letters to trace and an empty line beneath it.
K-303.p2: Every ending on this page is a plain s, which is deliberate: with words this long the child has enough to manage without a spelling change as well. Helicopters is twelve letters, and writing it once from a dashed model is a genuine piece of work for a five-year-old. Three pictures rather than two on the many side also matters - it stops the child reading the badge as a picture of the word two, and makes many mean more than one rather than exactly two.
K-303.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child trace, say the word, then write. Four long rows may be enough for one sitting; there is no harm in doing two rows now and two later. The first words page uses three short animal names if these are too long, and covers the es ending that this page leaves alone. The trace and write words page builds the handwriting stamina these plurals need, and the a or an page works on the small word in front.

K-306.h1: Circle the Right Word: Four Animal Cards, A or An
K-306.title: A or An Worksheet with Four Pictures - Animals | Free PDF
K-306.metaDescription: A or an worksheet with four large cards: say the animal name aloud and circle a or an underneath. An iguana, a tiger, a bat, a monkey. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-306.p1: Four cards fill this Kindergarten a or an page, two across and two down, and each one holds a single large animal picture with two white chips beneath it reading a and an. An iguana, a tiger, a bat, a monkey. No word is printed anywhere on the card, so the child has to name the animal before there is anything to decide, then listen to the sound that name begins with and circle the chip that belongs in front of it.
K-306.p2: Four cards means four decisions, and that is the right number for a first attempt at a rule the ear makes rather than the eye. Three of these animals take a and one takes an, which is enough of an imbalance that a child who circles the same chip every time will get most of them right and still be caught by the iguana. That is the moment to stop and stretch the first sound aloud. The pictures are large enough to name from across a table.
K-306.p3: Print the PDF free and run this as a spoken warm-up rather than silent seat work, since saying the animal is the whole method. Cover the chips, name all four pictures first, then uncover and circle. The eight picture version doubles the cards and moves to vehicles. Nothing has to be written on either page - only circled - so a child whose handwriting is still slow can still show what the ear already knows about a and an.

K-307.h1: Circle the Right Word: Eight Vehicle Cards, A or An
K-307.title: A or An Worksheet with Eight Pictures - Vehicles | Free PDF
K-307.metaDescription: A or an worksheet with eight vehicle cards: a ship, a skateboard, an ambulance, a bicycle and four more, each with a and an chips to circle. Free Kindergarten PDF.
K-307.p1: Eight vehicles, two chips under each. This Kindergarten a or an page runs four rows of two smaller cards - a ship, a skateboard, an ambulance, a bicycle, a canoe, a jeep, a yacht, a taxi - and under every picture sit the same two white chips, a and an. The child says the vehicle name, hears whether it starts with a vowel sound, and circles the chip that goes in front of it. Nothing is written and nothing is printed to read.
K-307.p2: Eight cards is long enough to show a pattern rather than a handful of separate answers. Most vehicles here take a, so the ambulance stands out, and that is the page working as intended: the child has to keep listening rather than settling into a rhythm. Vehicles are also a harder set than animals for this rule, because the vowel-sound names are rarer - which means the child who gets ambulance right has genuinely heard it rather than guessed from the picture.
K-307.p3: Print the PDF free and go through it aloud in two halves, four cards then four, rather than in one silent run. If a child circles without speaking, cover the chips and ask for the name first. The four picture version uses larger animal cards and fewer decisions for a first attempt at the rule. Once a and an are secure in speech, the singular and plural page works on the other end of the same noun, and the write the word page asks for the vehicle names in writing.

G1-251.h1: Read and Color: Four Sentences, Four Colors
G1-251.title: Read and Color Four Sentences for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-251.metaDescription: Read and color worksheet with four short sentences and four colors: color 2 giraffes blue, 3 parrots red, with one distractor on every strip. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-251.p1: Four sentences, four colors, and one extra animal on every strip. This 1st grade read and color page gives each card a single instruction - Tom colors 2 giraffes blue, Color 3 parrots red - above a small group of black and white line-art animals. Two giraffes and a meerkat. Three parrots and a lion. The color key sits in a dashed strip at the top with a swatch beside each of the four color words, and nothing else is printed.
G1-251.p2: Reading here has a consequence that shows. To color anything the child has to decode the animal name, the number word and the color word, and hold all three at once, and the spare animal on every strip means a child who colors whatever is there will get it wrong. Four cards and four colors keep that load fair for a reader who is still sounding words out. A colored meerkat says more about the reading than any tick would.
G1-251.p3: Print the PDF free on plain paper so crayons and markers both work, and leave the key uncovered - looking up green is reading, not cheating. Four is the shorter of the two read and color pages: the busy version uses six sentences, six colors, counts up to five and more than one distractor per strip. When these sentences are followed easily, the write the word page turns the same animals from reading into spelling.

G1-252.h1: Read and Color: A Busy Page with Six Colors
G1-252.title: Read and Color with Six Colors for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-252.metaDescription: Busy read and color worksheet: six sentences, six color words and crowded strips of line-art toys where two or three pictures are distractors. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-252.p1: Six cards, six colors and a crowd on every strip. This 1st grade read and color page uses black and white toys and objects - tractors, ufos, helicopters, drums, buckets, cacti - and each card asks for a count of three, four or five of one kind while two or three others sit alongside them. Orange, purple, blue, red, yellow and brown run across the key at the top, which is twice as many color words as the shorter version carries.
G1-252.p2: Crowding the strip is what makes this the harder page. When four of the eight pictures are tractors and the rest are not, the child cannot color by shape at a glance; the noun has to be read, the pictures matched to it, then counted to the number the sentence gives. Higher counts add a second demand, because five means checking rather than seeing. A teacher scanning the finished page reads the errors directly: a purple ufo too many is a counting slip, a purple tractor is a reading one.
G1-252.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child work down one column at a time; six cards at this density is a full session rather than a warm-up. Keep the color key in view throughout. The four sentence version halves the cards, the colors and the distractors if this page is too crowded, and the write the word page moves the same toys into spelling. For reading that builds sentences rather than follows them, try the unscramble the sentence page.

G1-255.h1: Number of the Day: Teen Numbers on a 0 to 20 Line
G1-255.title: Number of the Day Teen Numbers for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-255.metaDescription: Teen number of the day worksheet: one number from 11 to 19 shown as a word, in ten frames, in tallies, in tens and ones and on a 0 to 20 line. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-255.p1: The number in the white card at the top of this 1st grade number of the day page is a teen number - 11 on this copy - and every box below asks for that same number in another form. Write the number word on handwriting lines. Fill the boxes before and after it. Split it into tens and ones. Shade it in two ten frames. Mark it in tallies. Find it on a number line that runs 0 to 20. Then count on three and count back three.
G1-255.p2: Teen numbers are worth a page of their own because they are the ones children say without understanding. Eleven and twelve give no clue at all, and thirteen through nineteen say the ones digit first and the ten second. Filling the tens and ones box beside two ten frames is what makes eleven visibly one ten and one, and doing that eight ways in a single sitting is what turns a recited word into a quantity. The 0 to 20 line keeps the whole range in view.
G1-255.p3: Print the PDF free and use it as a five minute opener with a fresh number each morning; the page never changes, so the child spends the time on the mathematics rather than on the instructions. Ten frames and tallies appear only on this version. The ten more ten less page moves to a 0 to 30 line and base ten blocks, and the up to 99 page adds a second digit. The number line page then isolates the find-it-on-the-line box.

G1-256.h1: Number of the Day: Ten More and Ten Less
G1-256.title: Ten More Ten Less Number of the Day for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-256.metaDescription: Number of the day worksheet with ten more and ten less: two written equations, base ten blocks and a 0 to 30 number line for one two-digit number. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-256.p1: Two equations sit in the middle of this 1st grade number of the day page and they are the reason it exists: 14 + 10 = and 14 - 10 =, each with an empty box for the answer. Around them are the usual boxes - the number word on handwriting lines, the numbers before and after, tens and ones, a dot grid to draw the number in base ten blocks, a 0 to 30 line to mark it on, and rows of arrows to count on and count back.
G1-256.p2: Adding ten is where place value stops being a label and starts doing work. A child who writes 14 as one ten and four ones has the answer to 14 + 10 already in front of them, and a child who counts on ten ones to reach 24 has not yet joined the two boxes together. That is precisely what a teacher should look at here: the tens and ones box and the ten more box, read side by side. The block drawing gives the child something to move rather than count.
G1-256.p3: Print the PDF free and ask the child to say what changed and what stayed the same between 14 and 24 - the ones digit never moves. The teen version stays under 20 and uses ten frames instead of blocks if adding ten is still too far. The up to 99 page adds one more and one less alongside these two and stretches the line to 100. Number walls and doubles and halves put the same numbers to work in addition facts.

G1-257.h1: Number of the Day up to 99: Two-Digit Numbers, Four Equations
G1-257.title: Number of the Day up to 99 for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-257.metaDescription: Two-digit number of the day worksheet: numbers to 99, ten more and ten less plus one more and one less, a 0 to 100 line and counting on by tens. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-257.p1: Seventy-nine fills the card at the top left of this 1st grade number of the day page, and it is the two-digit end of the range that makes this version the hardest of the three. Four equations are stacked in one box - 79 + 10, 79 - 10, 79 + 1, 79 - 1 - beside the tens and ones split and a dot grid for base ten blocks. The number line below runs 0 to 100 with a label every ten, and the last box counts on by tens rather than by ones.
G1-257.p2: Putting one more and one less next to ten more and ten less is the whole argument of the page. The two pairs look alike and behave completely differently: one changes the digit on the right, ten changes the digit on the left, and a number ending in nine makes both of them interesting, because 79 + 1 crosses into eighty and 79 + 10 does not. Counting on by tens from 79 in the final box asks the child to do it again three times over.
G1-257.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child use the 0 to 100 line to check the four equations rather than treating it as a separate box. Numbers ending in 8 or 9 are the ones worth choosing when you set the day's number. The ten more ten less page keeps the same shape with a 0 to 30 line and two equations, and the teen version is where to go back to if tens and ones are still shaky. The number line page practises the landmark counting this one assumes.

G1-258.h1: Write the Word: The First Letter Is Already There
G1-258.title: Write the Word with a Word Bank for 1st Grade - Animals | Free PDF
G1-258.metaDescription: Write the word worksheet with the most support: a six-word bank at the top and the first letter already printed on each line beside the animal. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-258.p1: A word bank runs across the top of this 1st grade write the word page in a dashed orange strip - bat, fish, fox, iguana, moose, rabbit - and the help does not stop there. Each of the six cards below shows one animal beside a handwriting line with its first letter already printed in teal at the start. The child names the picture, finds the matching word in the bank, and copies it onto the line from the letter that is waiting.
G1-258.p2: Two supports at once make this the gentlest of the three write the word pages, and it is aimed at a child who can read the words but cannot yet spell them. The first letter does more than start the word: it narrows the bank. Even so, two words here begin with f, so fish and fox still have to be told apart by looking past that first letter - which is exactly the small piece of independent reading the page is built to require.
G1-258.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child cross words off the bank as they are used; six cards and six words means the last one can be reasoned out. Once copying from the bank is quick, the no first letter version keeps the bank but empties the line, and the plain lines version removes the bank altogether and asks for the spelling from the picture alone. The abc order page uses the same kind of picture cards for sorting rather than spelling.

G1-259.h1: Write the Word: A Word Bank and Eight Empty Lines
G1-259.title: Write the Word Bank Worksheet for 1st Grade - Vehicles | Free PDF
G1-259.metaDescription: Write the word worksheet with a word bank: eight vehicle words at the top and eight blank handwriting lines, with no first letter to start you off. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-259.p1: The bank is still here; the first letter is not. Eight vehicle words sit in the dashed strip at the top of this 1st grade write the word page - bicycle, boat, bulldozer, canoe, car, ferry, jeep, tractor - and the eight cards below each hold a picture and a completely empty handwriting line. The child names the vehicle, finds its word in the bank, and writes the whole thing out, first letter and all, with the model available but never on the line.
G1-259.p2: Removing the printed first letter turns a copying task into a matching one. The child now has to choose between eight words rather than the two or three a starting letter would leave, and this particular bank makes that choice a real one: a boat and a ferry are both boats, a car and a jeep are both cars, so the picture has to be read carefully before the word is. The bank keeps the spelling correct while the naming does the work.
G1-259.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child point at the bank word before writing, so the eyes travel once rather than letter by letter. Eight cards is a full page at this stage. The first letter version halves the choice for a child who is still finding the bank hard to search, and the plain lines version takes the bank away entirely. When the words come easily, the abc order page puts the same vehicle cards into alphabetical order.

G1-260.h1: Write the Word on Plain Lines: No Word Bank at All
G1-260.title: Write the Word No Word Bank for 1st Grade - Toys | Free Printable PDF
G1-260.metaDescription: Write the word worksheet with no support: eight toy pictures, eight plain handwriting lines, no word bank and no letter boxes at all. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-260.p1: Nothing is printed at the top of this 1st grade write the word page. No bank, no letters, no boxes to count into - only eight cards, each pairing one of eight toys with a plain handwriting line. A scooter, a rocket, a balloon, a truck, blocks, crayons, a spade, a chess piece. The child names what is there, listens to the sounds in order, and writes the word from those sounds alone. It is the hardest of the write the word pages by a distance.
G1-260.p2: Spelling from a picture reverses reading: the sounds come first and the letters have to be found for them. With no bank to check against, what lands on the line is the child's own phonics, which is the point - this page is a record rather than an exercise. Some of these pictures also have more than one honest name, so a child who writes scooter, moped or bike has read the picture correctly whatever the spelling does, and that is worth saying before marking anything.
G1-260.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for each word to be stretched aloud, sound by sound, before the pencil moves. Read the finished page for patterns rather than for a score: the vowels are usually the story, and eight words are enough to show one. If the spellings collapse, the word bank version supplies the correct words while keeping the naming, and the first letter version supports both ends. The abc order page is the next thing to do with these toy words.

G1-262.h1: ABC Order: Number Four Fruit Cards 1 to 4
G1-262.title: ABC Order with Four Words for 1st Grade - Fruits | Free PDF
G1-262.metaDescription: ABC order worksheet for beginners: an alphabet strip and four tilted fruit cards to number 1 to 4, with no lines to copy onto. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-262.p1: Four fruit cards, four dashed circles and no writing lines at all. This 1st grade abc order page prints the alphabet a to z in tinted cells across the top, then scatters persimmon, banana, watermelon and mango below it at slight angles, each with its word under the picture and a small orange circle in the corner. The child runs a finger along the strip, decides which word comes first, and writes 1, 2, 3 and 4 in the circles. That is the entire task.
G1-262.p2: Cutting the writing out is what makes this the entry point of the family. Ordering and copying are two different jobs, and a child who can do the first but not yet the second finishes this page having done the thinking. The four first letters here - b, m, p, w - are spread wide across the alphabet, so no comparison is close and the strip answers every question directly. Numbering in pencil also means a change of mind costs one rubbed-out digit.
G1-262.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child touch each word's first letter on the strip before writing anything. Check the circles, not the neatness. When four spaced letters are ordered without hesitation, the number them then write them version adds four lines to copy onto, and the same first letter version brings in two pairs that share a starting letter and have to be split on the second. The write the word page supplies the spelling all three rely on.

G1-263.h1: ABC Order: Number the Cards, Then Write Them on the Lines
G1-263.title: ABC Order Number Then Write for 1st Grade - Vehicles | Free PDF
G1-263.metaDescription: ABC order worksheet in two steps: number four vehicle cards in their dashed circles, then copy the words onto four numbered handwriting lines. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-263.p1: The cards get numbered first and copied second on this 1st grade abc order page. An alphabet strip runs across the top, four vehicle cards sit below it - skateboard, jet, canoe, yacht - each with its word printed and a dashed circle in the corner, and four numbered handwriting lines wait at the foot of the page. The child numbers the circles 1 to 4 using the strip, then writes the four words onto the lines in that order.
G1-263.p2: Splitting the page into two steps is what makes it teachable. Ordering happens in the circles, where a wrong answer costs nothing, and only then does the handwriting start. That separation also tells a teacher exactly what went wrong: circles right and lines wrong is a copying slip, circles wrong is an ordering one, and the two need completely different help. The first letters here - c, j, s, y - sit far enough apart in the alphabet that the strip settles every question.
G1-263.p3: Print the PDF free and check the four circles before the child begins to write, so a wrong order is not copied out neatly. The number the words version stops at the circles if writing four words is too much for now, and the same first letter version keeps the lines but makes two pairs share a first letter so the second letter decides. The write the word page is where these vehicle words get spelled rather than copied.

G1-264.h1: ABC Order When Words Start the Same: Baby, Boat, Scooter, Swing
G1-264.title: ABC Order Second Letter Worksheet for 1st Grade - Toys | Free PDF
G1-264.metaDescription: ABC order worksheet using the second letter: six toy cards where baby and boat both start with b and scooter and swing both start with s. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-264.p1: Two pairs on this 1st grade abc order page start with the same letter, and that is the whole difficulty. Six toys sit on cards under the alphabet strip - baby, scooter, boat, truck, swing, helicopter - each with a dashed circle in the corner, and six numbered lines run across the bottom. Baby and boat both begin with b. Scooter and swing both begin with s. The strip cannot separate either pair, so the child has to look at the second letter.
G1-264.p2: This is the step where alphabetical order becomes a method rather than a look-up. Up to now the first letter has always decided, and the alphabet strip has always answered; here the child has to hold the b fixed, move to the a of baby and the o of boat, and go back to the strip for those. It is the same reasoning a dictionary needs. Six cards with two ties is enough to make the rule necessary without turning the page into a puzzle.
G1-264.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child cover the first letter of a tied pair with a fingertip - what is left underneath is the comparison that matters. Number all six circles before writing any line. The four word version has no ties at all and is where to start if this one stalls, and the number then write version adds the lines at four cards rather than six. The write the word page supplies the spellings these lines ask the child to copy.

G1-266.h1: Number Walls to 10: Four Three-Course Addition Pyramids
G1-266.title: Number Walls to 10 for 1st Grade - Addition Pyramids | Free PDF
G1-266.metaDescription: Number walls worksheet with sums to 10: four small addition pyramids, three bricks printed on each base and three empty bricks to fill. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-266.p1: Every wall on this 1st grade number walls page tops out at ten or less. Four pyramids are printed three courses high, each with three numbers already in the bottom row - 1, 1, 1 on the first, 3, 2, 3 on the third - and three empty bricks outlined in dashed orange above them. The rule is given once at the head of the page: each brick is the sum of the two bricks under it. Add the pairs, fill the middle row, then add those to set the top.
G1-266.p2: Small numbers are what let the structure be the lesson. When every sum is within ten, the child is not held up by the arithmetic and can see the thing that makes a number wall different from a column of sums: the middle brick of the base gets used twice, once on the left and once on the right. That surprises children the first time, and it is easier to notice when adding 3 and 2 costs no effort. The top brick is only right if both bricks below it are.
G1-266.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child use counters or a number line for the first wall, then work the other three without. Four walls is a short page and can be finished in one sitting. When sums to ten are automatic, the build every row version adds a fourth course and ten bricks per wall, and the missing brick version knocks a number out of the base and asks the child to work downward. Doubles and halves practise the same facts from another direction.

G1-267.h1: Number Walls: Build Every Row of a Four-Course Wall
G1-267.title: Four Row Number Walls for 1st Grade - Addition Pyramids | Free PDF
G1-267.metaDescription: Four-course number walls worksheet: a base of four printed numbers and six empty bricks to fill on each of four addition pyramids. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-267.p1: Four courses instead of three. Each of the four number walls on this 1st grade page starts with four printed numbers along the bottom - 2, 1, 3, 1 on the first - and rises through three empty bricks, then two, then one, ten bricks in all with six of them to fill. No gaps anywhere in the base, so every wall can be built straight upward: add each neighbouring pair, write the answer above, and repeat on the row you have just made.
G1-267.p2: The extra course is not just two more sums; it changes what an error costs. A mistake in the second row now feeds two bricks above it rather than one, so the wrong number spreads as it climbs and the top brick is wrong for a reason three rows down. Children discover from this that checking as you go beats checking at the end. Working with a number you wrote yourself, rather than one printed for you, is also the harder half of the task.
G1-267.p3: Print the PDF free and suggest the child finishes an entire row across all four walls before starting the next; it makes the pattern of the structure obvious. Sums here stay within twenty. The walls to 10 version is the three-course page to fall back on, and the missing brick version keeps four courses but removes a number from the base so the child has to subtract downward to recover it. Number of the day works the same sums from a single number.

G1-268.h1: Number Walls: Find the Missing Brick in the Bottom Row
G1-268.title: Missing Brick Number Walls for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-268.metaDescription: Missing brick number walls worksheet: one bottom brick is blank and a number higher up is given, so the child subtracts downward before building. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-268.p1: One brick is missing from the bottom row of every wall on this 1st grade number walls page, and one brick further up is filled in. The first wall reads 4, 1, 2 and a blank along the base, with a 7 sitting in the second course above the last pair. Four four-course pyramids are laid out this way. Before any adding can start, the child has to work out what number joins the 2 to make 7 - and only then build the wall upward as usual.
G1-268.p2: That first step runs the other way from everything else on the page. Every other brick is found by adding two numbers below it; this one is found by taking a known brick apart, which is subtraction wearing an addition problem's clothes. It is the missing addend question - 2 and what makes 7 - and children who are fluent at adding often stall on it the first time. Once the base is complete the wall behaves normally, which is a fair reward for the harder opening.
G1-268.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child write the missing addend as a question, 2 plus what makes 7, before answering it; naming the operation is most of the difficulty. If the reverse step is too much, the build every row version keeps four courses with a complete base, and the walls to 10 version drops to three courses and smaller sums. Doubles and halves is a gentler place to meet the same take-apart thinking, and number of the day works the same range.

G1-270.h1: Doubles and Halves: First Steps with Groups to Count
G1-270.title: Doubles and Halves First Steps for 1st Grade - Animals | Free PDF
G1-270.metaDescription: Doubles and halves worksheet for beginners: four cards of animal pictures, two to double and two to halve, with small groups a child can count. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-270.p1: Foxes do the counting on this 1st grade doubles and halves page. Four cards, two marked double and two marked half, each hold a white box of animal pictures with an equation underneath. On the doubles cards a dashed teal line splits two matching groups of foxes and the fact below reads 3 + 3 = with an empty box. On the halves cards a dashed orange arrow cuts a bigger group in two and the line below reads 6 = and two empty boxes to fill.
G1-270.p2: Small numbers and countable pictures are what make this the starting point. Every group can be checked by eye - three foxes and three foxes, six foxes split into three and three - so the child sees the double and the half as the same picture read two ways before either becomes a remembered fact. The dashed line is doing quiet work here: it shows that halving means a fair split into two equal parts, not simply a smaller number.
G1-270.p3: Print the PDF free and let the child draw over the dashed line on a doubles card to see the mirror, then count each side. Four cards is short enough for a first sitting. The to 20 version is the next step - eight cards, no pictures at all, and doubles from five to ten with the matching halves. Number walls put these same small sums inside a pyramid, and the number line page is useful alongside for counting the halves out.

G1-271.h1: Doubles and Halves to 20: Numbers Only, Eight Cards
G1-271.title: Doubles and Halves to 20 for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-271.metaDescription: Doubles and halves worksheet to 20: eight cards of numbers only, doubles from 5 to 10 and halves of 10, 12, 14 and 16, each with a dotted work box. Free 1st grade PDF.
G1-271.p1: The pictures are gone. Where the animals, fruits and vehicles versions of this doubles and halves worksheet give the child a group to count, this 1st grade page gives numbers and an empty dotted work box above each one. Eight cards run down the page in two columns: four marked double - 8 + 8, 5 + 5, 10 + 10, 6 + 6 - and four marked half, where 16, 14, 12 and 10 each have to be split into two equal parts written in a pair of boxes.
G1-271.p2: Doubles are the addition facts children remember first and lean on hardest, because near doubles like 6 + 7 are built from them, and every half on this page is one of those same facts read backward. Setting them side by side makes the pair explicit: double 8 is 16 and half of 16 is 8 and 8. The dotted box above each fact is deliberately blank - a child who still needs to draw sixteen dots may, and stopping doing so is the visible sign the fact has been learned.
G1-271.p3: Print the PDF free and watch the work boxes rather than the answers; the page has done its job on the day they stay empty. All doubles here run from five to ten and all halves are even numbers to twenty. The first steps version returns to countable groups of animals if the numbers alone are too abstract. Number walls use these sums inside a structure, and the number of the day page reaches the same totals from a single number.

G1-274.h1: Where on the Number Line? 0 to 10 with Two Arrows a Line
G1-274.title: Number Line to 10 Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-274.metaDescription: Number line to 10 worksheet: lines labelled only at 0, 5 and 10 with two orange arrows each pointing at unlabelled ticks to name. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-274.p1: Every line on this 1st grade number lines page runs from 0 to 10 and carries just three printed numbers: 0, 5 and 10. A tick stands at every whole number in between, and two orange arrows point up at two of the unlabelled ones, each with an empty dashed box floating above it. The child finds the nearest printed landmark, counts on tick by tick to the arrow, and writes the number in the box. Two arrows a line, and no line asks for more.
G1-274.p2: Two arrows is a deliberate limit. The whole skill here is counting on from a landmark rather than starting again at zero, and a short line with few questions gives the child room to practise that without the page becoming a marathon. Watching the pencil tells you which method is in use: a finger sliding from 0 every time works and is slow, while a finger that lands on 5 and steps twice has understood what the printed labels are for.
G1-274.p3: Print the PDF free and ask the child to say aloud which label they counted from before writing each answer; that sentence is the thinking made audible. This is the shortest number line page in the set. The fewer labels version keeps three landmarks but stretches the line to 20, so the runs between them get longer, and the to 30 version widens the range again. Number of the day includes one of these lines among its boxes.

G1-275.h1: Number Line to 20: Only 0, 10 and 20 Are Printed
G1-275.title: Number Line to 20 Fewer Labels for 1st Grade | Free PDF
G1-275.metaDescription: Number line to 20 worksheet with fewer labels: only 0, 10 and 20 are printed and three arrows a line, so counting on runs further. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-275.p1: Only three numbers are printed on the lines of this 1st grade number line page: 0, 10 and 20. Ticks mark every whole number between them, four lines fill the page, and three orange arrows stand on each one with an empty dashed box above. Because the landmarks are ten apart rather than five, the count from the nearest label can run much further - an arrow near the middle of a stretch may be four or five ticks from anything printed.
G1-275.p2: Taking the fives away is a small edit that changes the reasoning. With a label every five, no tick is more than a couple of steps from help; with labels only at 0, 10 and 20, the child has to decide whether to count forward from 10 or backward from 20, and choosing the shorter route is the beginning of estimating. Twelve arrows across four lines is enough repetition for that choice to become a habit rather than a one-off.
G1-275.p3: Print the PDF free and ask for the landmark to be written beside the first box on each line, so the route is visible. If the longer runs cause miscounts, the 0 to 10 version keeps three labels on a much shorter line with two arrows each. The to 30 version restores a label every five but widens the range into the twenties. Number of the day and number walls are where these located numbers get added together.

G1-276.h1: Where on the Number Line? 0 to 30, Labelled Every Five
G1-276.title: Number Line to 30 Worksheet for 1st Grade | Free Printable PDF
G1-276.metaDescription: Number line to 30 worksheet: four lines labelled every five with three arrows each, taking counting on past twenty into the twenties. Free printable 1st grade PDF.
G1-276.p1: The line stretches to 30 on this 1st grade number lines page. Four lines fill the sheet, each labelled at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 with a tick at every number in between, and three orange arrows per line point at ticks with no number of their own. An empty dashed box waits above each arrow. The child picks the nearest printed five, counts on or back to the arrow, and writes what it points to - twelve answers in all.
G1-276.p2: Widening the range past twenty is the point of this version rather than any change of method. The twenties are where the number names finally behave - twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, all built the same way - and locating them on a line is how a child confirms that the pattern holds. Keeping a label every five means the counting stays short even at the far end, so the difficulty is in reading and naming the larger numbers, not in tracking a long run of ticks.
G1-276.p3: Print the PDF free and have the child read each answer aloud as it is written; hearing twenty-eight while pointing at it does more than the box alone. The fewer labels version is harder in a different way, with only three landmarks across a shorter line, and the 0 to 10 version is the place to begin. Number of the day places a single number on a line like this, and the dot to dot count on page practises the same twenties as a sequence.
